paper_title: ApexID: Hierarchical Learning for Multi-Species Animal Re-Identification

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Animal re-identification (Re-ID) must distinguish individuals across species and capture conditions. We introduce ApexID, a hierarchical SphereFace2-based loss that integrates global identity discrimination with balanced animal-category supervision. Using 132,533 images curated from 19 public datasets, we evaluate three model families and four objectives on four external datasets with observation-aware retrieval protocols. ApexID achieves a dataset-averaged Rank-1 accuracy of 64.89% with ConvNeXt-Small and an mAP of 32.54% with MIEW-ID, outperforming their pretrained reference models. On elephants, a category absent from animal Re-ID training, our ConvNeXt-Small variant achieves the highest retrieval performance among the fourteen evaluated configurations. Scores vary by backbone and dataset, and open-set evaluation reveals remaining discovery challenges. These findings support hierarchical category-identity learning to improve transfer to unseen datasets and species.

These findings support hierarchical categoryidentity learning to improve transfer to unseen datasets and species. Code, weights, and data splits are available in our GitHub repository. 1. Introduction Individual animal re-identification (Re-ID) supports noninvasive population monitoring, movement analysis, and behavioral research by matching individuals across sightings [13, 43]. Reliable matching must preserve subtle individual cues despite changes in pose, viewpoint, illumination, and time. representation shared across animal categories must also accommodate broad appearance differences while distinguishing individuals within each category. Standard identity-only objectives do not explicitly model the categoryidentity relationships present in multi-species annotations. Meanwhile, backgrounds and acquisition conditions may correlate with identity or dataset, creating contextual cues that may not persist across sightings. These challenges motivate category-aware identity learning from curated animal foregrounds. We introduce ApexID, multi-species animal Re-ID approach that maps curated animal foregrounds into shared embedding space. We train its encoders with the ApexID Hierarchical Loss, two-level categoryidentity objective based on SphereFace2 [46]. The loss combines global identity discrimination over learnable identity sub-centers with balanced category supervision. For hierarchical supervision, an identitys parent is broad animal category, such as whale. Once the foregrounds have been extracted, closedset retrieval ranks gallery images by cosine similarity between normalized embeddings alone. We harmonize animal category labels across 19 public datasets, apply dataset-specific near-duplicate filtering within identities, and segment the animal foregrounds. We manually review the images, create or correct masks where needed, and retain 132,533 images for training and validation. We compare four objectives on three backbones and include two unmodified animal Re-ID checkpoints as references. Across four external datasets, ConvNeXt-Small trained with our loss achieves the highest dataset-macro Rank-1 accuracy (64.89%) among the 14 configurations and dataset-macro mean average precision (mAP) of 30.84%. Both scores exceed those of the unmodified MIEW-ID v3 and MegaDescriptor-L checkpoints. MIEW-ID v3 finetuned with our loss achieves the highest dataset-macro mAP (32.54%), compared with 31.89% for the same backbone fine-tuned with SphereFace2. Gains vary by backbone and dataset. We also evaluate the embeddings in separate, dataset-adapted open-set protocol that uses calibrated similarities to associate queries with known identities and group 1 observations of novel individuals. Our contributions are threefold: ApexID models for multi-species Re-ID. We fine-tune ImageNet-pretrained ConvNeXt-Small and two animal Re-ID encoders, MIEW-ID v3 and MegaDescriptor-L, on curated foregrounds using the proposed loss. hierarchical categoryidentity objective. ApexID Hierarchical Loss augments global identity discrimination with balanced category-level supervision through separate learned proxy for each animal category. curated multi-source dataset. We harmonize annotations from 19 public datasets, remove unusable images, and retain 13,348 source-specific identities. We retain the source dataset and observation-group identifier for each image. Motivated by prior work on timeand similarityaware splitting [1], we assign each observation group wholly to either training or validation. 2. Related Work Shared animal Re-ID representations. WildlifeDatasets introduced MegaDescriptor and unified framework for learning across heterogeneous wildlife datasets [13]. MIEW-ID studies multi-species animal Re-ID [32], while OpenAnimals investigates the transfer of person Re-ID techniques to animals [24]. We evaluate category-aware supervision across MIEW-ID v3, MegaDescriptor-L, and ImageNet-pretrained ConvNeXt-Small. Recognition objectives. ArcFace applies fixed additive angular margin to the target class [16], while Dynamic ArcFace adapts this margin during training [26]. Sub-center ArcFace represents each identity with multiple learned centers [17], and SphereFace2 trains one binary classifier per identity [46]. Yang et al. [47] construct coarse proxies by clustering class proxies and also evaluate hierarchy defined by annotations. The ApexID Hierarchical Loss uses the annotated animal category as an additional prediction target, with one learned proxy per category, alongside subcenter SphereFace2 identity discrimination. and observation-aware Foregrounds evaluation. Rueda-Toicen et al. [40] examine background reliance and laterality in jaguar Re-ID, illustrating why retrieval scores alone do not identify the visual evidence driving match. ApexID applies foreground processing across multiple animal categories. WildlifeReID-10k uses timestamps when available and visual similarity otherwise to reduce overlap between partitions [1]. We follow this principle by keeping observation groups intact in both training validation and closed-set galleryquery splits. For our separate batch open-set analysis, we adapt the calibrated similarity and graph clustering used by ElBassat et al. [19] in their AnimalCLEF 2026 system. 3. Dataset Construction and Handling 3.1. Sources and Scope ApexID combines 19 public animal Re-ID datasets that vary in annotation, image quality, and observation metadata. For each image, we retain its source dataset, animal category, individual identity, and observation group. Each individual is identified by the combination of its source dataset and its local identity label. Animal categories represent broad categories shared across the datasets. Table 1 summarizes the curated corpus, and Supplementary Table 6 lists all sources. Table 1. Primary ApexID training and validation partitions. Identities are counted within each source dataset. Known-validation identities also appear in training through different observation groups.

Within each source dataset, an identity is eligible for the split if at least two images are labeled as the same identified animal. Limitations ApexID assumes two-level categoryidentity hierarchy, whose effectiveness may depend on the granularity and reliability of the animal category annotations. These categories represent broad animal types rather than consistent biological taxonomic level. In particular, they do not necessarily distinguish between species within the same broader animal category. For example, all individuals in the whale subset are assigned to single whale category, without distinguishing among whale species. This choice reflects the available annotations and uncertainty regarding specieslevel identification. 8 8. Conclusion that function animal Re-ID loss We presented the ApexID Hierarchical Loss, multispecies extends SphereFace2 by combining global identity discrimination with balanced category supervision. Observation-aware evaluation across three model families shows that ApexID improves closed-set retrieval over the original pretrained references, while its gains in open-set re-identification vary by backbone and dataset. Open-set analyses reveal complementary strengths and remaining discovery challenges. These findings support category-aware representations for wildlife re-identification and underscore the need to validate transfer across species and acquisition conditions.

sections.content: References use the main papers bibliography; table and figure numbering is shared across the main paper and supplementary material. A. Data Sources and Curation Details Table 6 expands the corpus summary in Sec. 3.1. Identity labels are source-specific; image and observation totals include both training and validation partitions. Curation sequence. When acquisition information is available we use it to separate test and training set images. Within-identity MegaDescriptor similarity is used to remove near-duplicate images before segmentation and partitioning. SAM 3 is prompted with an animal-category description, such as photo of giraffe; the highestconfidence valid mask is then applied with black background. V-Rush review checks image quality, masks, and annotations; MobileSAM bounding-box prompts and manual brush correction are used to refine incomplete masks. A.1. Training and Validation Partitioning An identity denotes an annotated individual animal. An observation groups images associated with an encounter, capture event, or acquisition sequence. Images from the same observation may share pose, illumination, background, and camera conditions, making image-level random partitioning susceptible to correlated samples across splits. We write val known for the known-identity validation partition and val unknown for the held-out-identity validation partition of Table 1. Following timeand similarityaware animal Re-ID evaluation [1], known-identity data are partitioned at the observation-group level. Fully dated identities spanning multiple calendar days use chronological suffix closest to 22.5% validation-image target while keeping earlier dates in training. For identities covered by verified filename or session parsers (CTai, Giraffes, IPanda50, NDD20, and NyalaData), deterministic subset of whole groups is selected to approach the same target. For all remaining identities, frozen DINOv2 features [31] are used to form within-identity connected components, with exact-duplicate links identified first. Multiimage components are assigned entirely to training; singleton (single-image) components may enter val known. Dataset-wise selection at 12.5% ratio routes complete unknown identities to val unknown without splitting their groups. An identity may therefore appear in both training and val known through different observation groups, but images sharing group always share partition. Because whole identities and whole observation groups are assigned together, small datasets with few groups per identity can exceed the nominal targets. AmvrakikosTurtles, ReunionTurtles, and ZakynthosTurtles therefore have more validation than training images  (Table 6)  . External subset scope. Table 2 describes subsets eligible for closed-set evaluation. Closed-set eligibility excludes identities with fewer than two observation groups. The separate open-set protocol may include such identities as novel queries and uses gallery-free setting for private jaguar data. Role construction for this protocol is specified in Sec. 5.2. B. Implementation and Metric Details Preprocessing and embedding extraction. All models use the same segmented source images, with checkpointspecific resizing and normalization. The ConvNeXt-Small preset uses RGB foreground images resized to 440 440 and normalized with ImageNet channel statistics. MIEWID v3 uses the same preprocessing; MegaDescriptor-L uses 384 384 inputs normalized with mean and standard deviation 0.5. ConvNeXt-Small adds learned linear projection to 2048-dimensional embedding, whereas MIEW-ID v3 (2152) and MegaDescriptor-L (1536) use their native embeddings. We keep the ConvNeXt-Small projection, discard all training classification heads, and ℓ2-normalize the extracted embeddings before evaluation. Frozen manifests and cached embeddings separate data preparation, feature extraction, and evaluation. This allows the same prepared samples and extracted representations to be reused across the relevant evaluation procedures without repeating inference. ConvNeXt-Small training preset. Batches use identityuniform KPK sampling, with = 16 identities and KPK = 4 images per identity (B = 64), following [22, 41]. When an identity has fewer than four available images, its images are sampled with replacement. This affects batch composition only; proxy objectives consider all training identities. Augmentation includes mild affine transforms and occasional grayscale conversion, blur, Gaussian noise, and pixel dropout. Validation uses deterministic resizing and normalization. Optimization. Metric Definitions and Secondary Analyses Image retrieval. We report Rank-1, cumulative matching characteristic (CMC) curves up to rank 50, mean average precision (mAP), mean inverse negative penalty (mINP) [48], and identity-balanced Rank-1 and mAP. Rank-k, equivalently CMC@k, is the fraction of queries with at least one correct match among the first ranked gallery images. Multiple images of one gallery identity occupy separate ranks. Average precision is the mean precision at the ranks of all relevant gallery images, where relevance denotes shared identity; mAP averages querylevel average precision. For each query, inverse negative penalty is the number of relevant gallery images divided by the rank of the last relevant image; mINP is its mean over queries. Identity-balanced metrics first average within each query identity and then equally across identities. Pairwise clustering F1. Consider unordered pairs of distinct query images. predicted-positive pair shares predicted label; ground-truth-positive pair shares true identity. True positives satisfy both conditions. Pairwise precision and recall are Ppair = TP/(TP + FP) and Rpair = TP/(TP + FN); their harmonic mean gives pairwise F1. This differs from the item-averaged B3 metric. Secondary analyses. We report same-category verification (AUROC, EER, and TAR at fixed FAR), embedding diagnostics, and robustness to limited galleries and samecategory distractors. Same-category distractors are negative matches of individuals of the same species. Conditional re2 trieval excludes queries lacking an eligible gallery positive and reports resulting query coverage.
